'''Keith Andrew Hunter''' (24 November 1951 – 24 October 2018) was a New Zealand [[Ocean chemistry|ocean chemist]] who was a professor of chemistry and pro-vice-chancellor of sciences, at the [[University of Otago]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Chris de Freitas and Keith Hunter: The great climate debate|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10740806|newspaper=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=2 October 2014|date = 25 July 2011}}</ref>

==Biography==
Born on 24 November 1951, Hunter was the son of Nevin Lindsay Hunter and Othle May Hunter (née Brenton).<ref name="ODT obituary"/> He was educated at [[Auckland Grammar School]], graduated from the [[University of Auckland]] with a first-class degree in chemistry in 1974, and completed his PhD at the [[University of East Anglia]] in 1977.<ref name="PVC">{{cite web|title=University appoints new Pro-Vice-Chancellor|url=http://www.otago.ac.nz/news/news/otago005680.html|website=[[University of Otago]]|access-date=2 October 2014|archive-date=6 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006112400/http://www.otago.ac.nz/news/news/otago005680.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> He then spent a year at the [[French Atomic Energy Commission]].<ref name="ODT obituary"/>

Hunter joined the Department of Chemistry at the [[University of Otago]] as a lecturer in 1979, rising to become a full professor in 1994.<ref name="ODT obituary"/><ref name="PVC"/> His research focused on trace metals in natural waters, particularly in the ocean, and chemical equilibria in marine and freshwater systems.<ref name="ODT obituary"/> He found that the productivity of [[phytoplankton]] in much of the oceans is limited by the availability of iron.<ref name="ODT obituary"/>

Hunter served a term as president of the New Zealand Institute of Chemistry, and was involved in the establishment of the [[NIWA]]/University of Otago Joint Institute for Oceanography in 1996.<ref name="ODT obituary"/><ref name="PVC"/> He was awarded the Prime Minister's Science Prize in 2011 and the [[Marsden Medal]] in 2014, and was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of New Zealand]] in 1997.<ref name="Royal Society">{{cite web |url=http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/organisation/academy/fellowship/fellows-1919-present/g-i/ |title=The Academy: G–I |date= |website= |publisher=Royal Society of New Zealand |access-date=12 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=NZ wildlife could one day be predator-free|url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11357604|newspaper=[[The New Zealand Herald]]|access-date=7 March 2016|date = 12 November 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Professor Keith Hunter|url=http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/organisation/council/keith-hunter/|website=[[Royal Society of New Zealand]]|access-date=2 October 2014}}</ref>

Hunter retired as pro vice chancellor of sciences at Otago in 2016 after six years in the position, and died at his home in [[Dunedin]] on 24 October 2018.<ref name="ODT obituary">{{cite news | url=https://www.pressreader.com/new-zealand/otago-daily-times/20181222/282415580394219 | title=Respected academic and climate change researcher | date=22 December 2018 | work=[[Otago Daily Times]] | access-date=22 April 2019 | first=Elena | last=McPhee}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.odt.co.nz/news/dunedin/campus/university-of-otago/former-uni-science-leader-keith-hunter-dies | title=Former uni science leader Keith Hunter dies | date=25 October 2018 | work=[[Otago Daily Times]] | access-date=22 April 2019}}</ref>

Notable students of Hunter include [[Tuifuisaʻa Patila Amosa]].<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Amosa |first=Patila |year=2015 |type=Doctoral thesis |title=The Dissolution Kinetics of Calcium Carbonate in Seawater: Development and Application of an Automated pH-stat Method for the Measurement of Dissolution Rates |publisher=OUR Archive, University of Otago |hdl=10523/5461}}</ref>
